newsitem.title: UK: UK trade data show few signs of pound's strength.
newsitem.headline: UK trade data show few signs of pound's strength.

text.p: Britain's trade deficit with the rest of the world is still showing no sign of the pain the soaring pound is inflicting on exporters.
But it is only a matter of time until the gap widens and more timely figures for trade with non-European Union countries may already be showing the first glimmers of deterioration.
"These figures are far from conclusive in showing UK exports suffering from the weight of sterling's rise," said Philip Shaw, economist at Investec Bank.

Britain's global trade deficit totalled 508 million stg in May, down from 989 million in April and well below most economists' forecasts. Its non-EU deficit was 713 million stg in June, up from 563 million in May.
Shaw said the pound's nearly continuous ascent over the last year has sustained the J-curve effect longer than expected. "But at some point the figures will deteriorate severely," he said.
Sterling has shot up more than 25 percent on a trade-weighted basis in just less than a year, pushing up exporters' prices.
So far, the J-curve effect has not unwound so the boost to the trade balance in value terms, as export prices rise but demand is slow to react, has not worn off. But it will soon.
Shaw said exporters have managed to limit the fall in volumes thanks to past currency hedging and cutting profit margins.
The fact that input prices are eight to nine percent down on a year ago is also helping although other costs such as wages are picking up.

"They are staving off falling margins by hedging and cutting margins. But that can't last indefinitely. It would be a major shock if the figures don't show real signs of damage in the last few months of the year," Shaw said.
James Mckay, economist at PaineWebber, said the non-EU figures were starting to feel the strain of the pound's relentless rise, even though the global figures do not.

He said non-EU exports were down 1.4 percent while imports rose 0.5 percent in June. "We are likely to see this trend of falling export volumes and rising import volumes continuing in the coming months," he said.
"Sterling is certainly starting to take its toll and I think its going to get a lot worse later in the year."
Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets, agreed deterioration of the terms of trade was inevitable.

"With the pound's strength clearly having a dampening impact on overseas demand for UK goods, and consumer spending at home growing strongly, it is only a matter of time before the trade position begins to worsen."
He forecast a current account of deficit of 10 billion pounds in 1998, up from four billion this year.
